questions.text: In what year was HashiCorp founded?
questions.note: 2012. Vagrant had already been out for two years by then, which is why the founding year and the first release do not line up.

questions.text: Which was HashiCorp's first product?
questions.note: Vagrant, in 2010, two years before the company existed. Packer followed in 2013, Terraform and Consul in 2014.

questions.text: Who co-founded HashiCorp with Armon Dadgar?
questions.note: Mitchell Hashimoto, and the company name is his surname rather than anything to do with a hash function.

questions.text: What is HashiCorp's published product design philosophy called?
questions.note: The Tao of HashiCorp — workflows over technologies, automation through codification, immutability. It is still what the product teams argue from.

questions.text: Which HashiCorp product was released first?
questions.note: Consul, in April 2014. Terraform followed three months later, Vault in April 2015, Nomad that September, and Boundary not until 2020.

questions.text: Which two products were announced together at HashiConf Digital 2020?
questions.note: Boundary and Waypoint, both at HashiConf Digital in October 2020: identity-based access, and application deploys.

questions.text: Which language are Terraform, Vault, Consul and Nomad written in?
questions.note: Go, all four. The single static binary is why a Consul agent or a Nomad client is one file to ship.

questions.text: What is HashiCorp's policy-as-code framework called?
questions.note: Sentinel, across the enterprise products. Rego is Open Policy Agent's language and Gatekeeper is OPA's Kubernetes admission controller — both real, neither HashiCorp's.

questions.text: In Vagrant, what is a packaged base image called?
questions.note: A box. It is what a Vagrantfile starts from, and Packer is what builds one.

questions.text: Which consensus protocol backs integrated storage in Vault, Consul and Nomad?
questions.note: Raft, in all three. Paxos is the ancestor Raft was written to be easier to understand than; Zab is ZooKeeper's.

questions.text: What is IBM's long-standing nickname?
questions.note: Big Blue. IBM never coined it; it is usually traced to the blue of the logo and of the mainframe cabinets.

questions.text: Which port does Vault's HTTP API listen on by default?
questions.note: 8200 for the API, 8201 for cluster traffic. 8500 is Consul's HTTP API and 4646 is Nomad's, which is what those two are doing in the list.

questions.text: By default, Vault splits its unseal key using which scheme?
questions.note: Shamir's Secret Sharing: the root key is split into shares and a threshold of them reconstructs it. Auto-unseal replaces the ceremony with a cloud KMS, but the default is still Shamir.

questions.text: What best describes a Vault dynamic secret?
answers: A credential generated on demand, with a lease
A secret shared between two apps
questions.note: Generated on demand and bound to a lease, so it expires whether or not anyone remembers to revoke it. That is the whole difference from a static value in the KV engine.

questions.text: In Nomad, what is the set of tasks that are always placed together on one client called?
questions.note: A task group. It is the same idea as a Kubernetes pod and deliberately not the same word — Nomad places an allocation of a group, and the group is what lands on one client.

questions.text: Which product scans code and systems for leaked secrets?
questions.note: Vault Radar. It looks through repositories, wikis and ticket systems for secrets that were never in Vault — the half of the problem Vault itself cannot see.

questions.text: Which licence did HashiCorp adopt for its products in August 2023?
questions.note: The Business Source License v1.1, announced on 10 August 2023 in place of MPL 2.0. It permits everything except a competing offering, and each release reverts to MPL four years on.

questions.text: Which open-source fork of Terraform was created in response to that licence change?
questions.note: OpenTofu. It was forked within days as OpenTF and renamed in September 2023 when it joined the Linux Foundation. Terragrunt is real, but it wraps Terraform rather than forking it.

questions.text: In April 2024, Terraform Cloud was renamed to what?
questions.note: HCP Terraform, on 22 April 2024, and only the name changed. Terraform Enterprise is still a separate self-hosted product, which is what makes it a fair distractor rather than a trick.

questions.text: In which year did IBM complete its acquisition of HashiCorp?
questions.note: 2025. It was announced on 24 April 2024 and closed on 27 February 2025, at an enterprise value of $6.4bn. 2024 takes most of the room because the announcement is the part everyone remembers.

questions.text: Which programming language was developed at IBM in the 1950s?
questions.note: Fortran, from John Backus's team at IBM, delivered in 1957. COBOL came out of a committee, LISP out of MIT, ALGOL out of an international group.

questions.text: Where is IBM's corporate headquarters?
questions.note: Armonk, in Westchester County, New York, since 1964. Austin, Raleigh and San Jose are all large IBM sites, which is why they are the other three.

questions.text: Which company did IBM acquire for about $34 billion in 2019?
questions.note: Red Hat, and it is still IBM's largest acquisition — roughly five times what it paid for HashiCorp.

questions.text: IBM's Deep Blue defeated which world chess champion in 1997?
questions.note: Garry Kasparov, 3½–2½ in the 1997 rematch. He had beaten the same machine in 1996, which is the part that gets forgotten.

questions.text: Which is the world's southernmost capital city?
questions.note: Wellington, at about 41°S. Hobart is a state capital and Christchurch is not a capital at all.

questions.text: The Merlion is the landmark of which city?
questions.note: Singapore. The lion's head is for Singapura, the lion city; the fish tail is for its beginnings as a fishing village.

questions.text: Which of these countries has the largest land area?
questions.note: Australia, about 7.7 million km² — more than twice India and about four times Indonesia.

questions.text: In Japan, "Golden Week" falls across which two months?
questions.note: Late April into the first week of May, where four public holidays fall close together. It is the hardest week of the year to book anything in Japan.
